records.title: Show HN: Automatic deduction of FlashAttention kernel from ~25 lines of SQL
records.author: alxmrs
records.storyText:
In this demo, we automatically deduce a FlashAttention kernel with ~25 lines of SQL, which just expresses vanilla attention. This is possible due to three portable SQL extensions that we’re building: - xarray-sql: a library that efficiently represents petabyte scale array datasets in the cloud as tables (relations). - ddx: a database extension that adds automatic differentiation in the style of JAX to standard SQL, assuming the above array data model. - einfold: a modular query planner for fast tensor contractions in vanilla SQL, again, assuming the above array data model.

My hope is that the relational model and algebra provide fresh perspectives on how we might do accelerator programming. Here, our thesis is that separating the logical layers in a tensor program from the physical layers is both more correct and more scalable.

If the Bitter Lesson is a central dogma of machine learning, then why not formalize it with relational algebra?

If this interests you and you’d like to tinker with us at the intersection of database theory and ML systems, join us on Discord at https://xql.systems (link at the bottom). Cheers.

records.storyText:
I have built a cosy fish tank simulation you can leave on a large screen and watch from time to time. I like pixel art but didn’t want to be religious about it, so I think of it as pixel art adjacent.

This summer, down with the flu, I started a small experiment. It ended up taking about 50-70 hours of my time, iterating over several months.

There is a 24-inch display in my kitchen powered by a used Lenovo mini PC (previously it was a RPi, but I had to upgrade to get a better GPU). I used it to show a rotation of my home photos, but now I’ve switched it to show this fish tank.

No prior game dev experience, but years of backend development and all the time spent reading indie dev blogs (honourable mentions Factorio and Banished) helped.

I used LLMs to give me a hand. It rather felt like playing a game, maybe like Factorio a bit, switching from system design to art direction and back and learning more about game dev to make it look better and better. For me it became a way to express creativity I might otherwise not have had time for. Along the way I learned what marine snow is and how fish swim. One funny story was me curiously asking an LLM if it could find some research papers on fish swimming patterns and styles and base the implementation on that, and it did.

I also used it to create a surprise for my wife’s birthday: on the day, three fish with QR codes appeared, each leading to a quest in the real world. But that is another story. Halloween is around the corner, so try the Halloween theme.

records.title: Show HN: A language model that lives in a boot sector
records.author: kerlenton
records.storyText:
All the ideas came from the boot sector demo scene where people had been writing chess and BASIC games in 512 bytes, even a C compiler. I wondered what one can do using a neural network instead of a program and generating boot logs for non-existent hardware was something fun to try.

Entire inference engine is 510 bytes of MBR, weights, vocab, and strings reside in the sectors following MBR. Small char-level neural network was trained on dmesg generated by machine, so machine produces Linux boot messages infinitely.

train.py performs precisely the same integer arithmetic operations as the asm code does and thus produces an output identical character-by-character to the one produced by QEMU. The difference analysis revealed my favorite bug. The characters at the beginning matched those generated by the simulator, but then the output diverged. I retrieved the hidden layer via QEMU’s debug port and compared the neurons' values with those of the simulator, one neuron at a time. Only the value of the first neuron was correct. The activation involves idiv, and idiv stores its remainder in edx. The pointer to the biases table was stored in edx, which resulted in the first neuron being biased correctly and the following ones using garbage. Now the bias' address is determined from the loop counter, and no pointers have to survive the division. Another bug I found simply by looking at the code before I did my first run-through: the BIOS print routine zeros out bx, but bx contains the predicted character number. This explains the push and pop of bx surrounding the print.

sectorllm is the most similar to my project, as it runs an actual 5-layer llama2 with attention mechanism in just 1.2K of assembly code. It is the trade-off in the opposite direction, as my engine needs to fit into one sector and therefore my network has just one hidden layer of int8 operations for dreaming the dmesg.

records.title: Show HN: Similarity, a spiritual successor to 2000s-era OkCupid
records.author: stickfigure
records.storyText:
This is a side project I've been working on on-and-off (mostly off) since the 1990s. I guess you would call it an experimental "dating site" though it's designed to be fun/interesting to people who aren't single (like me).

You don't need to sign in to see how it works, so try it out. There is no swiping.

The original inspiration was a 90s-era website called moviecritic.com that let you rate movies and get movie suggestions via collaborative filtering. I thought "hey, what about just matching me to the _people_ with the same taste instead?" And why just movies?

The closest thing to this was 2000s-era OkCupid, before it was Tinderized. I want to capture its appeal, while making something novel.

Similarity is not vibe coded, though I lean pretty heavily on codex (mostly the $20/mo plan - not a lot of tokens burnt here). The stack is java, guice/gwizard, elastic beanstalk, postgres (neon), react, jotai, and few cloudflare doodads. The match engine is a custom in-memory structure; getting the LLM to load test and optimize it was really a wow moment. Everything is PaaS and designed to scale by itself, cheaply, hands-off.

I'm working on some ideas to help with the chicken/egg problem but for now I have low expectations. It's cheap to run and I have a day job.

Would love feedback!

records.author: furqanrydhan
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Furqan founder of Nebula. We've spent a lot of time building, using and breaking browser agents. The main issues we ran into were costs and speed. So we built our own and open sourced it.

It's pretty simple, give it a task and it drives Chrome faster and cheaper than the alternatives.

At each step it lists the page's elements instead of screenshots. This means it can't click on buttons that aren't there.

We use System One models (currently Jev), which keeps costs extremely low, around 11x lower on average. If Jev does fail, we fall back to a cheap LLM like Gemini Flash Lite or Deepseek v4.1.

We ran our 46-task suite against Browser Use's hosted agent at its default settings. Each task ran three times, both on their cloud browsers. fastbrowse cost $0.030 a run, theirs cost $0.318. We passed 137 of 138 runs, and they passed 133.

To set up all you need is uv, Chrome, and a TypeSafe or OpenRouter key, both work:

uvx fastbrowse "What is the title of the top story right now?" --start https://news.ycombinator.com/ --local

Would love to hear feedback on it and how it's working for you guys.

https://github.com/agent-labs-dev/fastbrowse

records.title: Show HN: A Daily Poem Writing Puzzle
records.author: egglemonsoup
records.storyText:
Hello my beloved tech forum!

Earlier this year I moved to a new apartment, and scattered a box of poetry magnets all over my fridge. Whenever people came to visit, I noticed how they always loved making poems of their own, not to mention enjoying the poems others had already created. It became such a fun and entertaining tradition, (especially due to the range of creative messages that my friends chose) that I felt compelled to make a full stack project out of it.

While LLM agents have made the technical aspects of building a project like this easier, it took me a really long time to nail the algorithm for choosing daily word sets. I started with a huge collection (on the order of 100,000) of words, grouped by part of speech and sorted by the frequency of use in English. I tried randomly choosing a few words in the top 10, a few in the top 100, and so on, for each part of speech.

That straight up did not work. Trying to make poetry out of those wordsets felt terrible. It was very discouraging. I had to go back to the drawing board many times. My current solution came about when I found some databases of words, one sorted by their sensory value (from most to least sensory-evoking) and one where words are sorted on a spectrum of concreteness to abstractness.

Another key to picking fun and interesting word sets was ensuring there are a solid set of words that are included in every set no matter what. This "glue" set was handpicked by words that I found myself searching for over and over again when trying to write poems, but it is deliberately small to help people be creative in how they express ideas.

I used Deepseek v4.1 Flash and the Pi agent. My AGENTS.md emphasizes my status as a junior developer, specifically prompting the agent to never make architectural decisions on my behalf, to quiz me on the architecture/code involved before implementing changes I request, and to never write copy so I can make sure the site feels warm and genuine in my own words. I wanted to avoid letting the code get out of control for when I want to add features in the future.

One of the things I love about building these kinds of projects that LLMs enable is being able to add tiny features that most people will never see. For example, I added special effects that occur when a haiku is written.

I chose TanStack Start and React this time instead of SvelteKit. The experience was about the same. And kudos on poems are deliberately spammable. I like seeing number go up.

Friends have expressed enjoyment from using it so far, but I'm excited to hear feedback on y'all's experience and see if there's anything huge I'm missing. Thank you in advance!

records.title: Show HN: KuralHub 1.0, Speech emotion datasets for 70 languages in one place
records.author: luxshan_t
records.storyText:
Update to an earlier Show HN. KuralHub is a catalog of speech emotion datasets for the 70 most widely spoken languages, with benchmark results for 11 pretrained speech models on 33 of those datasets. Version 1.0 adds:

- A searchable catalog with one page per language. Each of the 90 datasets lists its emotion labels, size, licence, access link and citation. - All 363 benchmark runs as downloadable CSV and JSON, with the logs for each run. - The published paper (Interspeech 2026), and code that runs on current PyTorch and Transformers. - A short form for suggesting a missing dataset or a model to benchmark.

The most practical finding: the right model depends on the language. Whisper had the best average, but HuBERT came out on top for nine languages, bigger checkpoints did not help, and Tamil, Telugu and Kannada were hard for every model.

25 of the 70 languages still have no known emotional speech dataset, including Sinhala, Nepali, Hausa and Yoruba.

Catalog: https://aaivu.github.io/KuralHub/datasets.html Results: https://aaivu.github.io/KuralHub/benchmark.html What changed: https://github.com/aaivu/KuralHub/releases/tag/v1.0.0 Paper: https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2026/thavarasa26_in...

Suggestions for missing datasets are welcome, especially for those 25 languages, and so are new languages beyond the current 70.

records.title: Show HN: Imza – plan and review focused coding agent
records.author: umutsevdi
records.storyText:
Hi everyone. I've been building Imza for the last three months. It's yet another coding agent. I know there are a dozen have been posted here. But I believe this one is different enough to have a place here.

It has three explicit modes: plan, build and review. Plan mode allows you to draft a spec document together with the agent. Both you and the agent can edit the document until everything is clear. Build mode takes the plan and implements it. Review mode provides you a code review tool. You can annotate things you want to change in the code and send them as revision to the plan mode.

It's entirely written in C++, requires no account, supports 50+ providers including OpenAI subscriptions or local models. Imza supports MCP, skills and instruction files out of the box and uses 8-11MB RAM at startup.

One of the biggest differentiator is the Lua engine. What I did differently here is agent receives only one tool, that allows the LLM to execute Lua scripts. I then passed C++ methods as Lua bindings that the agent can execute. So model can orchestrate multiple bindings in one call. Each binding passes through a permission layer. Since Lua is the only way to interact with the filesystem, imza can monitor and control the model's behavior.

I'd love to hear your feedback. Thanks

Website: https://imza.run

Source: https://github.com/umutsevdi/imza

records.title: Show HN: Hashsync – Deduplicate SSH streams against the receiver's files
records.author: someplaceguy
records.storyText:
On a recent trip, while stuck on spotty hotel Wi-Fi and roaming 5G, I got fed up with how much bandwidth commands like rsync and nix-copy-closure waste.

rsync's delta transfer compares each file only with the file of the same name on the destination (or, with --fuzzy, a file in the same directory), so renamed, moved and copied files are sent in full.

nix-copy-closure can be worse: a rebuilt package gets a new store path, so the whole package is sent again, even when most of its contents haven't changed.

So I created hashsync, which runs a command over SSH and deduplicates the command's output, input, or both against an index of the receiving host's files.

As an example, for my last NixOS update, nix-copy-closure would have sent 1.7 GiB with --gzip, but hashsync took it down to 0.7 GiB instead. On some of my backups, I've seen up to 2x-10x less data and time to transfer compared to rsync with compression.

Two things make hashsync unique:

1. It searches at every byte offset of the stream, whatever its format, for blocks of the indexed files. In effect, it works like rsync's algorithm, but across every indexed file.

2. It's a transparent pipe, so it works with rsync, tar, or anything else you'd send through ssh.

See the repo's README for more info.

Feel free to try it out and let me know if you have any questions!

records.title: Show HN: Uncracked City, detective game where you question LLM suspects that lie
records.author: passkey1510
records.storyText:
I'm the developer. The game sends you to a city, you search the places for clues, then question the suspects with your own words, typed or spoken. Each suspect is played by an LLM that only knows its own character, its own timeline and what you've shown it; it never sees the solution. You catch a lie by showing a clue against a statement, and the case engine decides whether that pair is a contradiction, not the model. Then you write the report: who, when, where, why, with proof for each.

The hard parts were not the generation. They were keeping every case solvable (a solver checks each case before it ships: every lie must be catchable with the clues on the map), keeping the suspects from leaking the truth, and keeping the AI cost per player under control (typed questions are capped per day, voice replies are cached per line).

Stack: Godot 4 client, Node on Lambda, MongoDB, Anthropic models for the suspects, ElevenLabs and Soniox for voices. Solo, built in a short sprint, launched this week on Android, iPhone waiting for Apple's review. Free, no account.

I'd like to hear what breaks: a suspect that says something dumb, a case that is unfair, a lie the engine should have caught. There's a Flag button under every reply.

records.author: spacec0wb0y
records.storyText: I run muso.fm, a radio aggregator focused on finding the best music-centric internet radio stations around the world. I compiled a list of the best Halloween stations for non-stop Halloween spooky music and sounds to play. Halloween music, horror soundtracks, old-time radio dramas, ambient atmosphere, a kids' channel and some oddities. Hit play and leave it running for a party or while you work. records.title: Show HN: BeamDisk – High Performance iSCSI Initiator for macOS
records.author: nulledy
records.storyText:
Hey Everyone,

At work, and for several of our employees at home too, we've been big users of shared storage. We have a big TrueNAS storage server at the office containing a mix of spinning rust and flash. In addition to SMB and NFS, we've been big users of iSCSI for our Linux and Windows servers and clients.

But all of our employees use Macs, and due to the lack of modern iSCSI initiator software for Mac we were never able to utilize iSCSI for Mac clients. Existing legacy iSCSI initiators for Mac use kernel extensions that require turning off System Integrity Protection in recovery mode to install on Apple Silicon Macs.

That's insane. You shouldn't have to severely sacrifice your Mac's security to use iSCSI! So, we built a high performance user-mode iSCSI initiator for macOS. Our solution is a sandboxed Mac App Store application that requires no Kernel Extensions, no drivers, no reduced security and no reboots to install.

Introducing BeamDisk, the first high-performance user-mode iSCSI initiator for macOS without security compromises.

BeamDisk allows you to mount LUNs from your storage server, NAS, or Enterprise SAN arrays directly to your Mac and have them show up as standard disks. You can format the LUNs APFS, HFS+, any format you like.

BeamDisk can easily saturate a 10 Gigabit Ethernet connection and hits tens of thousands of random R/W IOPs on standard SATA SSDs. All of the benchmarks on our site were recorded on our own hardware on an M4 Mac Mini over 10 GbE with no special tricks.

Even just standard Time Machine backups to APFS LUNs are far more performant and MUCH more reliable than Time Machine over SMB.

Today, we're releasing our first public beta via Apple's TestFlight. Beta spots are currently limited to 100, first come first served. Beta users will have access to all features, for free, forever.

Once we land in the Mac App Store, BeamDisk will have a 30-day trial with all features unlocked and then will be free for basic Home users and paid ($25) for business use.

For you prosumers out there with massive homelabs (our kind of people) the free version's limits can be lifted via an in-app purchase once BeamDisk is on the App Store. For TestFlight testers everything is unlocked, forever.

Happy to answer any questions you have and collect feedback to share with the team. Otherwise, give it a shot and get your LUNs "Beamed" to your Mac!

BeamDisk.app - https://BeamDisk.app

Community GitHub Repo for Discussions, Issues, Roadmap, etc - https://github.com/3rdBitLabs/BeamDisk

Have a great weekend!

records.title: Show HN: Pollsight – a simple tool to aid ballot research
records.author: gaieges
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I built Pollsight, an simple civic web application that aims to solve the problem of the amount of time++research needed to vote based on your preferences on an overwhelming amount of races and referendums by collecting data from various sources and aggregating and summarizing that content in line with what you care about.

In Austin we have 53 Races, and 10 Propositions to vote on, and never enough time to devote to understand what each issue and candidate is about. So I built something to help with this process.

What it does is collects info from a number of different places: social media, candidate websites, OpenFEC, Vote411, and other places, and utilizes that using a RAG db + your preferred interests + AI to rank candidates most inline with your interests and with summaries (with sources) of the "why".

Would love feedback, especially on certain regions that don't have enough data (it's surprisingly hard to find everything!).

Hope this helps! Now get out there and vote!

records.title: Show HN: Teaching a 4M-param model to read like a child, with RL and no labels
records.author: rybthrow2
records.storyText:
I have been really interested in reinforcement learning and had a go at trying to teach a model through simulation to read and speak through experience.

It’s two small networks (~4M parameters total) trained on a MacBook. It passed generated versions of England’s Year 1 Phonics Screening Check (36.6/40, pass mark 32), and the bit I like most is that it taught itself irregular words like “glove” through reading practice. It was given 42 sound slots and the voice learned from transcribed recordings, so it’s not scaffolding-free. Details on that are in the post.
